rejected.title: Consumption and resource use
card: Consumption is the use of goods and services by people, households and businesses. When consumption rises, more resources are needed to make, move and sell what is bought.
Resources include water, energy, minerals, timber and farmland. Taking them out of the environment can use them up faster than nature can replace them.
Making and using goods also creates waste and greenhouse gas emissions. More consumption tends to mean more of both.
Wealthy countries tend to consume more per person, because people there can afford more goods, energy and travel. Their consumption also draws on resources from other countries through trade.
rejected.remember: More consumption means more demand for resources, and more waste and emissions.

a.q: Households in a city start buying new phones every year instead of every three years. What is the most likely effect?
opts: More demand for minerals, and more electronic waste
Less demand for minerals, as phones become cheaper
No change in resource use, as the phones are the same
Less waste, because newer phones are made more cleanly
a.why: Making more phones needs more minerals and energy, and old phones become waste sooner. Phones being cheaper does not cancel this: buying more of them still draws on more resources.
a.clue: Think about what is needed to make each extra phone.

b.q: Country X is wealthy and imports most of its clothing from factories in other countries. Why does its consumption still add to resource use and emissions?
opts: Making and shipping the clothes uses resources elsewhere
Imported clothes use no resources as they are made abroad
Only goods made at home count towards resource use
Emissions only happen where the clothes are worn
b.why: Demand from buyers in Country X drives the use of water, energy and materials in the countries that make the clothes, and shipping adds emissions. The tempting idea that imports are free of impact is wrong, because the resources are still used, just in another place.
b.clue: Where does the demand come from, and where are the goods made?

draft.title: Consumption and resource use
card: Consumption is the use of goods, energy and services by people and businesses. When it rises, more resources are needed to make, move and sell what is bought.

Resources are the materials and energy taken from the environment, such as water, minerals, timber and fossil fuels. Some, like fossil fuels and minerals, form too slowly to be replaced within a human lifetime.
Making, moving, using and throwing away goods also creates waste and greenhouse gas emissions. Higher consumption can mean more of both.

Wealthy countries tend to consume more per person, because households can afford more goods, energy and travel. Many of those goods are made abroad, so the resource use and emissions can happen in other countries.
draft.remember: Higher consumption raises demand for resources, and adds waste and emissions, wherever the goods are made.

a.q: Households in a city start replacing their phones every year instead of every three years. What is the most likely effect?
opts: More demand for minerals and more electronic waste
Less demand for minerals and less electronic waste
Steady demand for minerals but more electronic waste
More demand for minerals but less electronic waste
a.why: Making more phones needs more minerals and energy, and old phones become waste sooner. The tempting idea that demand for minerals stays steady ignores that each extra phone has to be made from new materials.
a.clue: Think about what is needed to make each extra phone, and what happens to the old one.

b.q: Country X is wealthy and buys most of its clothing from factories in other countries. How does this buying still add to resource use and emissions?
opts: Buyers' demand drives production and shipping overseas
Emissions occur where clothes are worn, not where made
Resource use stops once goods are made in another country
Shipping clothes by sea creates no emissions
b.why: Demand from buyers in Country X leads factories overseas to use water, energy and materials, and moving the clothes adds emissions. The idea that the impact leaves with the factory is tempting but wrong, because the resources are still used, just in another place.
b.clue: Ask where the demand comes from, and what happens before the clothes reach the shop.

a.best: More demand for minerals and more electronic waste

b.best: Buyers' demand drives production and shipping overseas

problems.detail: Why (a) says each extra phone 'has to be made from new materials'. That overstates it, because phones can contain recycled materials. 'Needs more materials' would be accurate.

Two distractors are plainly absurd for Year 12 ('Shipping clothes by sea creates no emissions', 'Resource use stops once goods are made in another country'). Students can rule them out without knowing the idea, which leaves the question too easy.
The correct option 'drives production and shipping overseas' is slightly unclear. It could be read as shipping going overseas rather than production happening overseas and goods being shipped in.

check.summary: The card and answers are sound. The why for (a) overstates that phones must be made from new materials, and question b has weak, obviously false distractors and slightly unclear wording in its correct option.

proposal.title: Consumption and resource use
card: Consumption is the use of goods, energy and services by people and businesses. When it rises, more resources are needed to make, move and sell what is bought.

Resources are the materials and energy taken from the environment, such as water, minerals, timber and fossil fuels. Some, like fossil fuels and minerals, form too slowly to be replaced within a human lifetime.
Making, moving, using and throwing away goods also creates waste and greenhouse gas emissions. Higher consumption can mean more of both.

Wealthy countries tend to consume more per person, because households can afford more goods, energy and travel. Many of those goods are made abroad, so the resource use and emissions can happen in other countries.
proposal.remember: Higher consumption raises demand for resources, and adds waste and emissions, wherever the goods are made.

a.q: Households in a city start replacing their phones every year instead of every three years. What is the most likely effect?
opts: More demand for minerals and more electronic waste
Less demand for minerals and less electronic waste
Steady demand for minerals but more electronic waste
More demand for minerals but less electronic waste
a.why: Making more phones needs more minerals and energy, and old phones become waste sooner. The tempting idea that demand for minerals stays steady ignores that each extra phone needs more materials to make.
a.clue: Think about what is needed to make each extra phone, and what happens to the old one.

b.q: Country X is wealthy and buys most of its clothing from factories in other countries. How does this buying still add to resource use and emissions?
opts: Its demand leads to production abroad and goods shipped in
Emissions occur where clothes are worn, not where made
The factories' own choices cause the impact, not its demand
Its imports add to resource use within Country X only
b.why: Buyers in Country X create the demand, so factories overseas use water, energy and materials, and shipping the clothes in adds emissions. Blaming only the factories is tempting, but they make the clothes because Country X buys them, so its consumption drives the impact.
b.clue: Ask why the factories make the clothes, and where that work happens.
